note: Four of five, and the one miss is the reason he did not buy — which makes this the most instructive ICP row in the batch. Matches successful on overwhelming circumstantial evidence rather than a stated occupation: constant international travel with named stops in Mykonos, Ibiza, Saint-Tropez and Marbella, 'back-to-back meetings all day', a 15-hour flight to Barcelona for a race, and elective stem cell therapy in place of shoulder surgery. Recorded as a match with the caveat that the rep never asked what he does, so the occupation test passes on inference; that omission is itself a finding, since it is the single question the ICP is built on. Matches income unambiguously and by self-declaration — $1,500 to $2,000 a month on personal trainers, and 'it's not even like the $4,000. I spend way more on stupid [stuff] all the time.' Matches good_to_great almost verbatim: 'I'm not here to lose 10% of body fat or anything like that. I'm just looking to change it up', with a plateau as the presenting complaint. Matches not_deconditioned emphatically — training twice a day, Hyrox competitor, former competitive lacrosse player. Misses neglected_health, and this is not a technicality. The criterion assumes health is the under-tended area of an otherwise successful life; for Jared it is the most tended area of his life. He has no neglect to correct, which is precisely why he rejected the accountability pillar ('I'm sure a lot of other clients, you got to get them to actually work out every day. I'm going to be doing that') and why he could only value the offer as a programming product. Edge rather than core because that single miss removes a third of the offer's value proposition and drove the entire objection. The rep reached the same conclusion himself at 00:10:26, before pitching anything: 'you're not our typical client.' Judged on criteria, not outcome — the call ended in a follow-up, and the rating would be the same either way.
